name: Swedana

lead: Swedana, from a Sanskrit word for perspiration, is an Ayurvedic steam or heat therapy. It is a preparatory step for the Panchakarma cleansing programme alongside oil massage (snehana).

Practitioners describe it as opening channels and relaxing the body; people who use it for appearance seek clearer, softer-feeling skin and relief of muscle stiffness. Research on its effects is small: a pilot study of whole-body swedana recorded short-term changes in blood pressure and pulse.

paras: Steam is applied to the body or sometimes with herbal additions, typically after oil massage, in a clinic or spa setting under a practitioner.

A pilot study recorded increases in blood pressure and pulse rate right after a session. People with heart or blood pressure conditions are generally advised to seek medical guidance before heat therapies.

angle.text: Practitioners present swedana as a relaxing heat treatment that leaves skin warm and refreshed. The appearance benefits are described by users rather than measured.

lead: Swedana (also Svedana) is an Ayurvedic treatment whose name comes from the Sanskrit for 'perspire'; it is also described as steam therapy or fomentation [1]. Steam is applied, sometimes with herbal additions, and the therapy is a preparation for Panchakarma, along with snehana [1].

People use it for a sweat-induced feeling of relaxation and a refreshed look to skin. In Ayurveda, sweating is thought to open channels in the body (srotas), whose blockage is said to cause disease [2].
Reference works note that Ayurveda's theory and practice are regarded as pseudoscientific by some critics [2]; swedana itself has been studied in small observational and add-on trials.

paras: Swedana is performed after oil application in Panchakarma and can be local or whole-body (Sarvanga Swedana) [1][3].

A pilot observational study of Sarvanga Swedana found a significant rise in blood pressure and pulse rate immediately after therapy, and a reduction in systolic pressure and pulse on continued sessions in a subgroup [3]. A randomized open-label study of 70 chronic heart failure patients tested a Panchakarma-based protocol that included swedana as add-on to standard care and reported increases in METs and peak oxygen uptake [4]. These studies did not assess appearance.

Because passive heat changes blood pressure and heart rate, as seen in the pilot study, those effects are documented [3]. Wikipedia notes that some Ayurvedic preparations contain toxic metals, which concerns herbal products rather than steam itself [2].
